title: Evidence Edit: New Findings on Attainment Grouping and Independent Learning
author: EEF Editorial Team
summary: The EEF's May 2026 Evidence Edit presents a new UCL Institute for Education study on maths attainment grouping across 97 English schools, providing the most current evidence from the English system on a perennially contested question. The study found that mixed-attainment maths classes produce one month's less progress on average compared to setted classes, with the negative effect concentrated entirely among high-prior-attainment pupils (two months' less progress); pupils with lower prior attainment and socio-economically disadvantaged pupils made similar progress in either grouping arrangement. The newsletter also presents the EEF's seven-step model for building genuine independence: activating prior knowledge, explicit strategy instruction, modelling thinking and processes, checking understanding, guided practice, independent practice, and structured reflection—framing independence as a deliberately transferred responsibility, not a state achieved by leaving pupils to work alone. An implementation guidance section emphasizes that what ultimately matters is how an approach manifests in day-to-day school work, not just its theoretical promise. A new large-scale wellbeing trial is announced: Place2Be's Learning Together for Mental Health, a whole-school programme targeting secondary schools across England.
points: The UCL/EEF study across 97 English schools found attainment-based grouping in maths does not harm lower-prior-attainment or socio-economically disadvantaged pupils (similar progress in either arrangement) but significantly benefits high-prior-attainment pupils, who gain the equivalent of two months' additional progress in setted classes.

The overall school-level effect of mixed-attainment maths classes is one month's less progress—a meaningful negative result driven entirely by suppressing high-attainment pupils, not by harming lower-attainment groups—which reframes the equity argument: setting is not inequitable to disadvantaged pupils in this dataset.

The EEF's seven-step independent learning model frames independence as a graduated transfer of responsibility from teacher to pupil—not a state achieved through unstructured solo work—requiring explicit strategy instruction and modelling before guided and independent practice.

EEF's implementation guidance emphasizes that effective change requires structured but flexible processes tailored to the day-to-day realities of each school; a good idea in principle will fail without intentional implementation planning and ongoing adjustment.

EEF is recruiting secondary schools in England for a large-scale trial of Place2Be's Learning Together for Mental Health, a whole-school programme using restorative practice and pupil voice to improve relationships, wellbeing, attendance, behaviour, and attainment.
quotes: Teaching maths in sets does not appear to harm the progress of pupils with lower prior attainment, or socio-economically disadvantaged pupils. These groups made similar progress whether they were taught in mixed-attainment maths classes or in classes that were set by attainment.

Pupils with higher prior attainment in maths who were taught in mixed-attainment maths classes made less progress than those taught in setted maths classes. (Equivalent to about two months' less progress.)
Independence isn't developed by leaving pupils to work alone—it's built through explicit teaching and modelling.
An educational approach or idea may seem great in principle, but what really matters is how it manifests itself in the day-to-day work of people in schools.
